listen.explanationKey: What are three rights of everyone living in the United States?
facts: Some rights belong to everyone living in the United States, not only to citizens. Most of these rights come from the First Amendment.
Freedom of expression: you can share your ideas in many ways, like writing, art or speaking.
Freedom of speech: you can say what you think, even if you disagree with the government.
Freedom of assembly: you can meet together with other people in a peaceful group.
Freedom to petition the government: you can ask the government to change a law or fix a problem.
Freedom of religion: you can practice any religion, or no religion at all.
The right to bear arms: the Second Amendment protects the right to have guns, following the law.
For the test, you need to name three.

story.say: Some rights belong to everyone living in the United States, not only to citizens.

help.simpler: These rights are for everyone living here, citizens or not.
help.example: A person who just moved to the United States has these rights too.
help.why: The test asks you to name three rights of everyone living in the United States.

story.say: Most of these rights come from the First Amendment.

help.simpler: The First Amendment is the first amendment in the Bill of Rights.
help.example: It protects speech, religion, the press, meeting in groups and asking the government for change.
help.why: Knowing the First Amendment helps you remember most of these rights.

check.statement: These rights are only for U.S. citizens.

story.say: Freedom of expression: you can share your ideas in many ways, like writing, art or speaking.

help.simpler: You can show what you think in many ways.
help.example: You can write a story, paint a picture or sing a song about your ideas.
help.why: “Freedom of expression” is one right you can name on the test.

story.say: Freedom of speech: you can say what you think, even if you disagree with the government.

help.simpler: You can say your opinion out loud, even about the government.
help.example: You can tell a reporter you think a new law is unfair.
help.why: “Freedom of speech” is another right you can name.

story.say: Freedom of assembly: you can meet together with other people in a peaceful group.

help.example: Neighbors can meet in a park to talk about a problem in their town.
help.why: “Freedom of assembly” is another right you can name.

check.prompt: Tap the right to meet together in a peaceful group.

story.say: Freedom to petition the government: you can ask the government to change a law or fix a problem.

help.simpler: You can ask the government for a change.
help.example: People can sign a letter asking the city to fix a dangerous road.
help.why: “Freedom to petition the government” is another right you can name.

story.say: Freedom of religion: you can practice any religion, or no religion at all.

help.simpler: You can choose your religion, or have none.
help.example: People can pray at a church, mosque, temple or synagogue, or not pray at all.
help.why: “Freedom of religion” is another right you can name.

story.say: The right to bear arms: the Second Amendment protects the right to have guns, following the law.

help.simpler: “Bear arms” means to have and carry guns. People may own guns if they follow the law.
help.example: There are laws about who may buy a gun and where guns may be carried.
help.why: “The right to bear arms” is another right you can name.

check.prompt: Which one is a right of everyone living in the United States?

story.say: For the test, you need to name three.

help.simpler: The officer asks for three rights. Say three of them.
help.example: You could say: “Freedom of speech, freedom of religion and freedom of assembly.”
help.why: Practice saying three together so they come easily.

listen.explanationKey: Who can vote in federal elections, run for federal office, and serve on a jury in the United States?
facts: Only U.S. citizens can vote in federal elections, run for federal office and serve on a jury.
Four amendments to the Constitution are about who can vote.
They say that a male citizen of any race can vote, that women can vote, that no one has to pay a tax to vote, and that citizens 18 and older can vote.

story.say: Only U.S. citizens can vote in federal elections, run for federal office and serve on a jury.

help.simpler: These three things are only for U.S. citizens.
help.example: Voting for President, running for Congress and serving on a jury are for citizens only.
help.why: The test asks who can do these three things. The answer is U.S. citizens.

check.prompt: Tap the one that happens in a courtroom.

story.say: Four amendments to the Constitution are about who can vote.

help.simpler: Four changes to the Constitution say who can vote.
help.example: Over time, these amendments let more people vote.
help.why: The test asks you to describe one of them.

story.say: One says a male citizen of any race can vote.

help.simpler: This amendment said race cannot stop a male citizen from voting.
help.example: This is the 15th Amendment, from 1870, after the Civil War.
help.why: “A male citizen of any race can vote” is one answer on the test.

help.simpler: Women got the right to vote in every state.
help.example: This is the 19th Amendment, from 1920. The photo shows a march for women’s right to vote in 1913.
help.why: “Any citizen can vote. Women and men can vote” is another answer on the test.

check.prompt: Who can vote in federal elections?
choices: Anyone who lives in the United States
Only people born in the United States

story.say: One says no one has to pay a tax to vote.

help.simpler: No one can be charged money to vote.
help.example: Some places once charged a “poll tax.” The 24th Amendment ended that in 1964.
help.why: “You don’t have to pay a poll tax to vote” is another answer on the test.

story.say: And one says citizens 18 and older can vote.

help.example: Before the 26th Amendment in 1971, many states made voters wait until 21.
help.why: “Citizens eighteen and older can vote” is another answer on the test.

check.prompt: Tap the amendment about citizens 18 and older.
